localChanges: In Civilization II games, Diplomats and Spies can steal advances, sabotage, incite a revolt and bribe a unit, and a Spy can also poison a city's water or plant a nuclear device, choose which advance to steal or which building to sabotage (or leave it to chance), and escape to fight again. The incite window says what each price does to a treaty (#1007).

In Civilization II games, a mission under a treaty asks first, and an agent lost on one causes an incident: when a foreign agent is caught at work against you under a treaty, you choose whether to go to war (or end the alliance) or let it pass, and under the Republic or Democracy an incident of your own can bring a Senate scandal and Anarchy (#1007).

In Civilization II games, Caravans and Freight set up trade routes, whose deliveries pay research as well as gold, and the city screen names each route's partner and goods. Computer players send Caravans, Diplomats and Spies too (#1007).
In Civilization II games, you're told when water is poisoned, an agent is caught or lost, a planted nuclear device goes off or is found out, and what an incident comes to (#1007).

In Civilization II, computer players now build Caravans and Freight and send them to set up trade routes with the best partner they can reach, ferrying them overseas when there is none at home. They never use a Caravan to help build a Wonder.

Computer players' Diplomats and Spies now go to the cities of players they have no treaty with and carry out the mission the original game would choose there: stealing an advance, sabotage, poisoning the water or inciting a revolt. They never break a treaty doing it, and they leave a city alone once their player signs a treaty with its owner.
